transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 15:30 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Northbridge), Marcus Grey (Northbridge CTO), Sofia Ruiz (QB engineer)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on unit economics for hosted vs dedicated vs private. Customer needs clarity on per-token unit costs, batching/caching levers, latency tradeoffs, and an initial budget target (~$12k/mo). Agreed next steps: share pricing model, run bench, and review security docs.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros?
[00:06] Lena: hi lena here, head of ai for northbridge, we run quant models and a lot of text summarization for research.
[00:12] Marcus: marcus, cto, want to understand infra implications.
[00:16] Sofia: sofia, quant eng, i'll own the bench work.
[00:20] Jordan: jordan from redwood, i'll cover perf and batching details.
[00:24] Maya: great. goal today is to understand your usage patterns and map to cost levers — hosted vs dedicated vs private, and what a pilot would look like.

[00:45] Lena: high level, we expect ~250k generated tokens/day across users, peaks up to 500k. mostly short prompts (50-200 tokens) with some long-run summaries (1k-2k). budget target about $12k/month to start.

[01:10] Jordan: ok that's helpful. so on hosted we price per-token — for reference, our hosted gen price examples are in the sheet i'll send, but e.g. ballpark for standard models is $0.0025 per 1k input tokens and $0.006 per 1k output tokens, applied to total tokens. dedicated moves to reserved throughput pricing — commit for capacity and you get much lower unit economics via amortized GPU costs and batching.

[01:40] Marcus: can you explain the batching and cache effects? like how much can we realistically shave off per-token?

[01:47] Jordan: sure. two big levers: batching at runtime and prefix/KV cache. batching groups requests within a short window, increasing GPU utilization — that reduces cost per token because you amortize overhead. depending on latency SLOs you can see 1.5x-3x effective throughput improvements. caching (we call prefix and kv cache) holds repeated context so you're not re-sending or re-computing same prefixes, that can drive down token compute by 20-60% on high repetition workloads.

[02:20] Sofia: our workload has a lot of repeated system prompts and similar user prompts — seems like caching could help a lot. how do you measure cache hit rate?

[02:28] Jordan: we provide dashboards with token hit/miss and cache efficiency. in practice for prompt-heavy apps we often see 30-50% hit rate after warm-up. note transcription: sometimes titles show kv cash in logs, haha, transcription typo.

[02:48] Marcus: for dedicated, what's the commitment look like and how predictable is latency?

[02:55] Maya: dedicated is reserved GPU pools with SLA-backed targets. typical contracts start with monthly commits and scale to annual. latency is much more predictable because you control the pool and routing; plus we can tune batching policies to balance cost and p99 latency.

[03:18] Lena: quant question: if we use quantized models on dedicated, do you still need the same GPU class? we were thinking 8-bit/4-bit to reduce cost.

[03:27] Jordan: yes quantization reduces memory and can allow denser packing on smaller GPUs. our runtime supports mixed precision and quantized kernels. cost improvements depend on model and throughput, but 20-40% reduction in GPU hours is common. caveat: small quality delta sometimes. we recommend running a quant eval on your prompts.

[03:50] [04:00] Marcus: ok, give me an example calc — if we have 250k gen tokens/day and assume 40% caching and 2x batching improvement, what's monthly cost hosted vs dedicated?

[04:10] Jordan: quick back-of-envelope: 250k tokens/day -> 7.5M tokens/month. if 40% cache hit, effective billed tokens ~4.5M. with hosted example rates of $0.006 per 1k output tokens (and we're simplifying to output-only for calc), that's 4.5M / 1000 * $0.006 = $27. OK that's too low because i'm only using output price; include input tokens and service fees, rough hosted could be $600-$1,200/month for that profile on small models. but for higher-res models or more complex generation it'll rise. dedicated: with a reserved 1-2 GPU pool amortized plus infra maybe $6k-$9k/mo but gives consistent p50/p95 and much lower marginal unit cost at scale.

[04:55] Lena: those numbers seem inconsistent with our expectations — we were modeling $10k+ hosted for 7M tokens. are we missing something?

[05:05] Maya: yes worth clarifying — the per-token numbers vary by model family. the example i gave was for smaller open models; large Llama/opt-class or tuned models can be 5-10x higher. also embeddings and multimodal ops are billed differently. we should run a tailored calc: please share token histograms and model/quality targets, and we'll map to concrete pricing.

[05:30] Sofia: what about private (VPC/on-prem) — security is sensitive for us, but what's the cost delta?

[05:37] Jordan: private deployments have platform fee + infra + support. on-prem has higher setup/time costs, but you get full control and can use existing hardware which may reduce long-term unit costs if you're running at high utilization. a typical small private engagement starts higher (setup + licenses) e.g., $15k-$30k initial setup then lower monthly ops if infra is customer-provided.

[06:05] Marcus: latency targets — we need p95 < 400ms on short prompts. can the runtime meet that on hosted?

[06:12] Jordan: depends on model and region and whether you accept warm GPUs vs cold starts. with streaming and optimized kernels we hit p95 < 300-400ms on smaller models for short prompts in our nearest region — dedicated makes that much more stable. we'll include p95 numbers from our benchmarks in the sheet.

[06:35] Lena: any hidden costs — egress, storage, or logging?

[06:39] Maya: good call. egress is cloud provider-level if you have large data movement; we also have optional longer-term eval storage for metrics which is an add-on. audit logs and retention policies can influence billing if you enable high retention volumes. we'll call those out in the pricing sheet.

[06:58] [07:10] Sofia: how do you handle bursty traffic? we have heavy intraday spikes.

[07:15] Jordan: hosted supports autoscaling but there can be cold capacity limits; dedicated supports burst capacity and reserved burst buffers. routing policies can also spill to fallback model variants to keep latency/p95 in-range while controlling cost.

[07:35] Marcus: what about model variants — are cheaper models first-class for routing?

[07:40] Jordan: yes you can configure policy-based routing: latency-first to lower-res model, cost-first to cheapest compatible, or region-based. automatic fallback to a quantized/sharded variant is supported.

[08:00] Lena: okay can you walk through a concrete example of our monthly number target $12k? how to allocate between hosted vs dedicated pilot?

[08:12] Maya: one approach: start hosted pilot for 30 days with strict caching and batching configs plus telemetry. if hit rate and batching show good savings, transition to a small dedicated reserved pool for steady-state. initial pilot might be under $2k for testing and benching; dedicated reserve to meet production at your scale could be $6k-$9k/mo, leaving room in $12k target for growth and add-ons.

[08:45] Sofia: for the pilot, what data do you need from us?

[08:48] Jordan: sample prompts, token histogram, typical latencies, and a few representative workflows. we'll run bench with our perf harness and produce cost per 1k tokens under different configs.

[09:05] Maya: action items recap: maya to send pricing sheet and sample calc, jordan to configure bench and propose test times, lena to share token histogram and permission for a small benchmarking op.

[09:22] Marcus: on compliance, can you send SOC2 and SSO doc?

[09:26] Maya: yes will include SOC2, SAML/SSO integration notes, KMS/HSM options and audit log config in the packet.

[09:40] Lena: are there any common gotchas you see when customers move from hosted to dedicated?

[09:44] Jordan: two big ones — underestimating cache warm-up time (initial runs show lower hit rates) and not tuning batching windows for interactive latency. also people forget to account for infra reservation granularity which can force a higher baseline if you pick too-large GPU types. we help with sizing guidance.

[10:10] Sofia: ok let's schedule the bench run next week, mornings PST.

[10:15] Maya: i'll send calendar invites after i share the pricing sheet. any other questions?

[10:22] Lena: no, thanks very useful.

[10:25] Marcus: good session.

[10:28] Maya: thanks all — next steps as discussed.

End transcript. Note: transcript has occasional mis-hearings and shorthand ('kv cash', 'QB engineer') consistent with automated transcription.
